15 Games Like 'Total War' You Definitely Need to Play
Button Mash
15 Great Strategy Games You Need To Play If You Love The 'Total War' Series
Kyle Townsend
Updated September 23, 2021
Easily one of the biggest and most acclaimed strategy series of all time, it's hard to find games that are on the same level as Total War. With 14 releases under its belt, the Total War franchise continues to dominate the RTS genre, and with the latest installment, Total War Saga: Troy, the series has probably covered more historical events than your local history professor. While good strategy games are hard to come by (especially good historical ones), this list features 15 amazing games like Total War that are worth playing.
With stellar series like Rome, Shogun, and Medieval, the competition really needs to be considered "high strategy" to come anywhere close to the level of detail and complexity Total War features in each of its offerings, so not every strategy game compares. Fortunately, there are some amazing examples of real-time, turn-based, and tactical battle simulation games that explore all aspects of historical combat.
While most of these games are PC-only, there are plenty of great games like Total War on the PS4 and Xbox One as well. Conquer's Blade and Romance of the Three Kingdoms XIV (which is definitely recommended for fans of Total War: Attila ) are two great examples that hold up just as well on other consoles. Check out the list below and vote up all the games you've played (and liked). Who knows, you just might find a new favorite RTS epic.
1
10 VOTES
Civilization IV
Photo:Firaxis Games
Metacritic score: 94
Sid Meier's Civilization games have been around for decades, and with each entry in the franchise, new and important features are added or tweaked. As a result, their evolution over the years pretty much guarantees that each subsequent entry will be better than the last. Civilization VI is no exception, as it stands as arguably the best game in the franchise. The game features added civilizations unseen in previous titles, alterations on the civics and tech trees, and many more improvements make it incredibly fun to play.
Why It's Worth Playing: While the turn-based strategy format is different from the Total War franchise, you can't get any more "grand strategy" than a Civ game. Each game sets the player up with a leader who commands their entire civilization through the various ages to one of five victory conditions. You command an army, navy, and air force, but you'll also instruct building projects, trade concerns, politics, economics, and everything else that goes into running a civilization. It's ridiculously complex, but engrossing and entertaining at the same time.
Developer: Firaxis Games, Soren Johnson
Platform: OS X, Macintosh, Microsoft Windows

Mount & Blade Warband
Photo:TaleWorlds Entertainment
Metacritic score: 78
Mount & Blade is a medieval strategy game with action role-playing elements, with the standalone expansion Warband being the most popular. The series features two epic DLCs, with Warband: Napoleonic Wars often cited as the best (though Viking Conquest is arguably just as great). That said, while Warband was ported to the PS4 and Xbox One in 2016, the two expansions weren't included. Gameplay is focused on horse-mounted combat, where the player gives orders to their Warband in the field. You can command archers to hold their position, or switch your infantry to blunt weapons — the sky's the limit, and the combat system is top-notch.
Why It's Worth Playing: Gameplay is different from the Total War franchise in that it is a sandbox role-playing game. The setting is the medieval land of Calradia, so historical accuracy isn't the name of the game for base gameplay. The Napoleonic Wars expansion is more of a multiplayer-focused add-on that is historically accurate. The battles can feature up to 220 different types of historical units, with is nothing short of stunning when you're running about the battlefield.
Developer: TaleWorlds Entertainment
Platform: Microsoft Windows, Linux, MacOS, PlayStation 4, Xbox One

Europa Universalis IV
Photo:Paradox Interactive
Metacritic score: 87
Europa Universalis IV is a grand strategy game and the fourth in the Europa Universalis series. The game revolves around the player's control of a nation from the Late Middle Ages through to the Early Modern Period (1441 to 1821). The game focuses heavily on warfare, but also includes everything from trade and the political administration of cities to diplomacy and colonization.
Why It's Worth Playing: Europa Universalis IV has some of the most innovative AI in the genre, and it helps to make for an outstanding experience. More than that, players need to be aware of everything going on in the world around them, so honing your strategy means more than simply moving one army to attack another. It's virtually impossible to become bored playing this game, as there are tons of responsibilities the player needs to address, ensuring their attention is constantly being called upon for things like border expansion, border protection, the gathering of resources, and the management of an empire.
Additionally, there are a ton of expansions for this game, which add new people, leaders, weapons, tactics, and more.

Crusader Kings II
Photo:Paradox Interactive
Metacritic score: 82
Crusader Kings II is a grand strategy game set in the Middle Ages. It's the first sequel in a trilogy of games, and as such features a handful of advancements over the original (which is also great). Gameplay is set within the years 1066 and 1452, though DLC and expansions have pushed the starting year as far back as 769. That means you can actually play as Charlemagne, but there are many more historical figures a player can choose.
Why It's Worth Playing: Crusader Kings II is insanely realistic, and gameplay comes to an end when the character dies without an heir to succeed them. This happens when all landed titled of the count rank, or above, are stripped. Hitting 1453 will also switch gameplay into an observer mode. Players can choose to play as a minor duke or count, but they also have the option of playing historical figureheads like William the Conqueror, Charlemagne, Genghis Khan, Harold Godwinson, Robert Guiscard, Robert the Bruce, Harald Hardrada, El Cid, Constantine X Doukas, Harun al-Rashid, Alexios I Komnenos, Richard the Lionheart, Ivar the Boneless, Alfred the Great, Baldwin I of Jerusalem, Boleslaw the Bold, and Saladin... to name a few.
Gameplay and success are entirely up to the player. There is only one in-game objective, which is to obtain prestige and piety points with the goal of surpassing historical numbers achieved by the actual leaders.
Developer: Paradox Development Studio

9. Age of Wonders III
Aerial view of paradise
Want your empire-building with fantasy flair? Look no further than Age of Wonders III.
In the Blessed Continent, races vie for supremacy. The human Commonwealth Empire desire the assimilation of the entire world under their rule. Opposing them are the High Elven Court, who wish to marshal the ancient races in opposition to the Empire’s expansionist ambitions.
After choosing one of the six races, you pick a leader, whom you level up like you would an RPG character – through questing and monster-slaying.
There’s an enormous world to explore, filled with secrets that can either help or destroy you. Expansion is achieved through conquest or diplomacy; exploitation of resources and opportunities; the strategic use of your forces; and, of course, the annihilation of rival powers.
One of the most enthralling games like Civilization on the market!
